h: A republic at war with itself: the picture before Ramlila Maidan
dek: Badri Raina, who has taught at Delhi University, argues that the MLC election results, the Supreme Court's firmness and the dissent inside the Election Commission together show that the ground is shifting under those in power.
body: In this piece, written just before the 1 November rally at Ramlila Maidan, Badri Raina begins with the recent Legislative Council (MLC) elections. The Prime Minister mocked the Congress for not winning a single seat. Raina calls this a childish taunt.

According to the writer, the BJP lost in Nagpur, the stronghold of Fadnavis, Gadkari and the Sangh. Both seats in Varanasi slipped out of BJP hands, and in Gorakhpur, Yogi Adityanath's party survived by only about three hundred votes. Of Uttar Pradesh's 11 seats, the SP alone took five, and its winning margins were far bigger than the BJP's slim wins. Raina reads this as a warning for the 2027 Assembly elections. The opposition asks: if paper ballots are so reliable, why not use them for all the elections ahead?

The article also records the obstacles on the way to the rally. Traders asked for it to be postponed, citing festival losses, even though the BJP's procession had passed through Chandni Chowk unhindered. The Cockroach Janta Party backed the rally despite police harshness and repeated its demand to remove Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, and students are holding firm on several campuses, Jamia among them.

For Raina the most important front is the court. On 28 October the Supreme Court told the Commission plainly that it understands everything. The court is examining the Form 6 rules, the claims of 'logical discrepancies', and the centralisation of the software used to add and delete names in the voter list. The writer asks how the Commission can call its decisions unanimous when two commissioners have written 14 dissent notes after decisions.

Finally, he speaks of the softness of corporate media and the bureaucracy's habit of 'betting both ways'. His conclusion is that the republic is at war with itself right now, and that only public activism can bring it back to the path of the Constitution.
nazar: Raina's piece takes the movement from the street to the counting table and the courtroom. That is its strength: the questions behind the slogan, namely which name was deleted by which software and with whose consent, are now on record in court. It may be hasty to draw big political conclusions from the MLC results, but this much is clear: the pressure for accountability is no longer just the opposition's demand.

However big the crowd at Ramlila Maidan, the test will be whether workers, Dalits, Muslims and migrants, whose names are alleged to be deleted first, stay at the centre of this fight or only in the count.
sawal: After fourteen dissent notes, what is left of 'unanimity'?
ref: Legislative Council (MLC) elections
Some states have an upper house alongside the Assembly. Some of its seats are elected from graduate, teacher and local body constituencies, and the results show the mood of educated voters.
Form 6
The application to enter a new voter's name. It is alleged that the Commission added conditions to it without changing the rules, which two commissioners objected to.
ank: Dissent notes recorded inside the Commission
SP seats in the UP MLC elections

h: Bengal's 16 lakh appeals: five holes in the Commission's explanation
dek: The Wire's Aparna Bhattacharya examines the Election Commission's affidavit in the Supreme Court and shows that the authority behind the appeals, which put lakhs of approved voters back in the dock, is not established.
body: About 16.10 lakh appeals were filed in West Bengal against voters whom judicial officers had found valid. On 26 October the Commission told the Supreme Court in an affidavit that these appeals were filed under the Representation of the People Act by officers of the state Chief Electoral Officer's office. Aparna Bhattacharya's analysis shows that this explanation does not hold up on five counts.

First, the 19 tribunals to which these appeals went were created by the Supreme Court, not by the law. Under the law, the appeal route runs from the ERO to the District Magistrate and then to the Chief Electoral Officer. Prasenjit Bose, chairman of the Bengal Congress's SIR committee, argues that the authority of the law cannot be stretched to a body the law does not even mention. Second, the court's April orders speak generally of 'officers' of the Commission and name no post.

Third, the affidavit lists legal officers but nowhere says that they filed the appeals. In the notices of one tribunal in Murshidabad, the appellant is recorded as the Additional Chief Electoral Officer. Fourth, in the records compiled by the Civic Research Group, more than 12 lakh appeals carry the same series code, meaning they were filed in a single batch on 5 April, a day before the order now being used to justify them.

Fifth, the Commission itself accepts that these voters are on the roll and were entitled to contest and vote in the recent election, yet it does not say on what ground they were challenged. In a file note of 12 August, Commissioner Sukhbir Singh Sandhu had asked exactly this: who was given the right to appeal.

Bose calls for these appeals to be dismissed as prima facie illegal and for a judicial inquiry. Whether the appeals were machine-generated or not, according to the piece, only an audit of the portal can tell.
nazar: This analysis puts documents in place of slogans, and that is why it carries weight. Putting a voter whom a judge has already accepted back in the dock without giving a reason hurts most those who have no lawyer, time or papers: Bengal's migrant workers, Muslims in border districts, and poor women.
sawal: Same day, same code: who filed twelve lakh appeals?
ref: Appellate tribunals (Bengal)
Bodies set up on the Supreme Court's direction to hear disputes over names deleted or added in the SIR, staffed by retired judges. On 20 March the Commission notified 19 tribunals.
ECINET
The Election Commission's centralised digital portal through which voter list work is run. Its audit records could show who filed an application and how.

h: That the young need a leash is an illusion of old parties
dek: Venkat P.S. Vemuri argues that those in power, the opposition and TV are all irritated by the Cockroach Janta Party because it is tied to nobody's peg.
body: In this piece, written on 10 October, the day of the Jantar Mantar protest, Venkat P.S. Vemuri says the Cockroach Janta Party troubles not just the government. The old parties, their friendly analysts and TV anchors are also uneasy because this movement has stood up on its own and asks for nobody's umbrella. According to the writer, being independent is not proof of conspiracy or immaturity.

The movement's grievances are concrete: leaked exam papers and allegations of tampering with voter lists. After this same campaign against the NEET leak, Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan had to resign. Now the demand is for the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. The BJP spoke of a foreign hand and anarchy, and the writer's reply is direct: put out the evidence if you have it, because stamping a label does not end questions.

The opposition is not spared either. According to the writer, it too is looking for who owns the movement and who its leader will be. He credits Rahul Gandhi with connecting to workers, students and farmers and standing with the young, but supporting is not leading, and the Congress has still not built an organisation beyond the family.

The piece is sharp on the action that day: thousands detained, the metro stopped, barricades on roads and mobile internet shut in several areas. The writer calls the dragging of women along the road barbaric and compares it with the methods of the Emergency, though he admits the situation is not exactly the same.

Vemuri also says the movement must improve its methods, firm up its allegations and sustain its organisation. But his conclusion is that it will be judged by its deeds, and parties and commentators with tainted records of their own are in no position to lecture the young.
nazar: This piece points at the old habit of first trying to prove that every popular surge is some party's pawn. Discussing the movement's weaknesses is necessary, but the first question should remain who leaked the paper and who deleted the names, not whom the sloganeer is connected to.
sawal: Is one who takes no party's umbrella an orphan?
ref: NEET-UG leak (2026)

The case of leaked papers in the national medical entrance exam, against which the students' movement from which the Cockroach Janta Party emerged was launched. Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigned on 25 July.

h: Cockroach away from the ballot: whose gain, whose loss?
dek: Saurabh Shukla's analysis is that the Cockroach Janta Party's decision not to contest elections is both a strategy and an excuse, and that if it enters the field, the Aam Aadmi Party will lose the most.
body: About two crore Instagram followers in five months, two big gatherings on Delhi's streets and the resignation of a Union minister: acknowledging this strength of the Cockroach Janta Party, Saurabh Shukla asks why it stays away from elections. On 12 October the police removed Jantar Mantar from the list of protest sites, and the leaders are tangled in detention and bail bonds.

Founder Abhijit Dipke has said that forming a party is not the solution for now, and on 25 September he asked the opposition not to contest elections at all, because in his view the elections are being rigged. Shukla argues that this claim of rigging gives the movement a permanent excuse never to contest, and that no major opposition party took the advice anyway. In a survey in August, 33 per cent of people appeared ready to vote for it and 43 per cent were not.

Then the piece turns to the allegations of ties with the Aam Aadmi Party. Dipke was a volunteer in the AAP's social media team from 2020 to 2023, and Delhi Chief Minister Rekha Gupta called it the AAP's 'B-team', while some BJP and Congress leaders have also called it an AAP pawn. Dipke denies every link.

The real arithmetic is of votes. In the 2025 Delhi election the BJP got 45.56 and the AAP 43.57 per cent of the vote. Shukla gives an illustration, not a prediction: if most of the votes of a new party with five per cent came from the AAP, the BJP's lead would grow to two to four points.

There is a question about Punjab too, where the AAP governs. The movement audited schools there, but no protest was seen over the murder of an anti-drug activist in Mansa. The writer concludes that Punjab's 2027 election will decide whether the movement goes beyond audits and sit-ins.
nazar: This piece is a critic of the movement, and that is why it is worth reading: one test of any popular surge is whether it asks its friends' governments questions just as hard. But the 'B-team' debate cannot cover the larger question from which this movement came: if trust in the voter list itself is gone, what use is the count of who wins and who loses?
sawal: Whose lead will five per cent of the vote double?
ref: CJP-Democratic
A separate faction formed on 3 September by a former volunteer, Manish Brahmbhatt, which accused the movement of closeness to the AAP. These allegations are unproven.

h: Dhaka, Kathmandu, Lima and now Delhi: the Gen Z wave
dek: Suddhabrata Deb Roy places the Cockroach movement in a chain of youth rebellions across the world and says that the government's repression and then its backing down both show its weakness.
body: From Bangladesh, Nepal, Kenya, Peru and Morocco to France and Serbia, the generation born between 1997 and 2012 is on the streets. Suddhabrata Deb Roy argues that India has now joined this wave. In a country with an average age of about 29, the burden of unemployment and insecurity falls on this generation, and social media is its organisation.

The spark came from the NEET-UG 2026 paper leak. According to the writer, this was the second such case in two to three years, and he blames the centralisation of the National Testing Agency. At a Supreme Court hearing on 15 May the word 'cockroach' came up for young people, and Abhijit Dipke made an online platform mocking exactly that, which became a movement within a few weeks.

The piece records a string of events: the sit-in at Jantar Mantar from 20 June, Sonam Wangchuk's 26-day fast, the 'Sansad Chalo' of 20 July, which met with lathis, tear gas and an internet shutdown, and the Education Minister's resignation on 25 July. Along with it came FIRs, allegations of foreign money, and pressure on the families of delivery workers. On the other side, left student organisations, farmers' unions, Nihang groups, mosques and gurdwaras came together.

Deb Roy sees this as different from the Anna movement of 2011: it is scattered and secular, and it turns into weapons the very things called the generation's weaknesses, such as satire, online agility and disorder. He also records Anand Teltumbde's warning that the choice of symbols and too much of a Gandhi take could blunt its edge.

The writer's conclusion is that the government's repression and then the minister's resignation both show its nervousness, but cases and harassment continue, so the outcome is still open. This piece is the first part of a series that explains the ground before the current anti-Election Commission phase.
nazar: Seen on the world map, this movement looks not like one party's move but like a generation's restlessness. The experience of Sri Lanka, Bangladesh and Nepal also shows that toppling power is the easy part. The hard part is whose table the rights of the poor, minorities and workers reach afterwards.
sawal: How far can a movement go on memes and disorder?
ref: Gen Z uprisings
Youth-led movements since 2022 in South Asia, Africa, Latin America and Europe. In Sri Lanka, Bangladesh and Nepal they changed governments.

h: The wound Ambedkar warned of in 1949
dek: S.N. Sahu argues that the written objections of two election commissioners themselves show that the Commission is running at one man's will, which goes against the thinking of both Gandhi and Ambedkar.
body: S.N. Sahu starts from 1931, when Gandhi in 'Young India' called adult franchise the foundation of Swaraj, a tool with which the common man keeps a rein on the powerful. According to the writer, tampering with voter lists, which the movement calls 'vote chori', blunts this very tool.

Then he goes to the Constituent Assembly of 15 June 1949. Introducing the draft of today's Article 324, Ambedkar had warned that injustice in preparing the voter list would cut at the roots of democratic government. Sahu says that same warning stands before us today.

The piece rests on an Indian Express investigation, according to which Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi recorded written objections 14 times in ten months. The issues were adding, deleting and restoring names and access to voter list data. It is alleged that Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar took decisions on these alone.

Sahu reminds us that all commissioners are equal and the Chief Commissioner is only first among equals. Decisions should be by consensus or majority. In the 1995 T.N. Seshan case the Supreme Court said that Article 324 gives the responsibility for elections to the Commission, not to any one person. According to the writer, decisions taken alone are a direct violation of this judgment.

His conclusion is that such conduct has made the Commission suspect and has wounded the democratic dream of Gandhi and Ambedkar. This piece predates the movement's 10 October phase, but the constitutional basis of its demand is clearly visible here.
nazar: Today, when the Commission tells the court that its decisions are unanimous, this piece sets the Constituent Assembly debate and the Seshan judgment against that claim. The voter list is not a technical register: not being on it, especially for poor, Dalit and Muslim citizens, is like being thrown out of the republic.
sawal: After the Seshan judgment, how does the Chief Commissioner alone get his way?
ref: T.N. Seshan v. Union of India (1995)
The Supreme Court judgment that upheld a multi-member Election Commission. The court said the Chief Commissioner's status is not above the other commissioners, and decisions will be by majority.
Article 324
The article of the Constitution that gives the Election Commission full responsibility for conducting elections, preparing the voter list and supervision.

h: Memes, a fast and Gandhi at the gate of Gujarat University
dek: Jesuit priest and human rights activist Cedric Prakash writes from Ahmedabad that in this Gen Z movement he sees the same edge of 'do or die' that there was in 1942.
body: Cedric Prakash's commentary is from Ahmedabad, where Gandhi Jayanti this time was marked differently from the official ritual. On 2 October more than two hundred young people gathered at the gate of Gujarat University and demanded the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner and the government, with slogans against rape culture and patriarchy as well. According to the writer, the police stood and watched.

Prakash recalls that the word 'cockroach' came up in a court hearing on 15 May, and a satirical platform built on it reached tens of lakhs of people. In July hundreds of students marched in Ahmedabad, some were detained, and on 25 July the Education Minister resigned, which the writer sees as only the first step.

The writer hears in these young people an echo of Gandhi at Gowalia Tank Maidan in August 1942. The difference is in method: sit-ins and fasts along with memes, songs, dark humour and Instagram videos, which also became an answer to disinformation. He calls their press conference at the Press Club in Delhi on 7 October more sensible than the Prime Minister's press conferences.

On the question of money, one protester said sarcastically that the money comes from the PM CARES Fund. Prakash says nobody believes this, but it turned the debate around, because that fund's accounts are still not public. He accepts that the earlier movements of farmers and human rights activists were also big, but this generation's scale and willingness to take risks are different.

His conclusion is that the government is rattled and has no answer except the police. This generation stands against corruption, communalism, exclusion and the flaws in the education and election systems, and Prakash is confident that it is showing the way toward a country of constitutional values.
nazar: That this voice is coming from Gujarat is news in itself, where spaces for protest have been shrinking for years. This hopeful piece is also somewhat hasty, but it reminds us that the movement's moral ground is being built not only at the Delhi sit-in, but at the gates and lanes of small towns too.
sawal: Why did the PM CARES jibe turn the debate around?
ref: Gowalia Tank Maidan (1942)
The Mumbai ground, now August Kranti Maidan, where on 8 August 1942 Gandhi gave the slogan 'Do or die' and began the Quit India movement.
PM CARES Fund
A relief fund in the Prime Minister's name, created in 2020. Questions have been raised continually about keeping it outside government audit and the right to information.

h: A 'people's impeachment' at 10 Rajaji Marg: six charges against Gyanesh Kumar
dek: At a symbolic parliament held at Kharge's home, with Meira Kumar in the chair, a motion to remove the Chief Election Commissioner was moved. At the heart of the charges is the claim that 13.2 crore names were deleted.
body: On Saturday, at 10 Rajaji Marg in Delhi, the official residence of Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge, the INDIA bloc held a 'public impeachment' of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. This was not Parliament. It was a symbolic gathering modelled on Parliament, chaired by former Lok Sabha Speaker Meira Kumar. Rahul Gandhi, Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha, was also present.

Opening the proceedings, Meira Kumar said the right to vote is the soul of democracy and that questions raised over the deletion of crores of names have so far gone unanswered. Kharge then moved a motion to remove Gyanesh Kumar and listed six charges in it.

According to The Tribune, the charges are: conspiring to influence national and state elections, removing 13.2 crore names from voter lists, changing Form 6 without parliamentary oversight, taking control of the lists through ECINet, keeping the other two Election Commissioners out of key decisions, and acting at the bidding of Prime Minister Modi and Home Minister Amit Shah.

Kharge said the right to vote, guaranteed under Article 326, is in danger. He reminded the gathering that seven months ago 193 opposition MPs had given notice to remove the Commissioner, which was rejected, and claimed that the bloc's MPs represent 60 per cent of the country's population. He demanded that all data related to the SIR, including the list of dead voters and deleted names, be made public. He also alleged that trains were stopped, the internet was shut down and young people were arrested to suppress the movement. The report records no response from the Election Commission or the government.
nazar: After the notice was rejected in Parliament, the opposition took the same debate to the public. It has no legal effect, but it put the charges in one place, in one document. It is now the Commission's turn to respond, and its silence will also be read as an answer.
sawal: Which of the six charges will the Commission answer first?
ref: Article 326
This article of the Constitution gives every citizen above 18 the right to vote on the basis of adult suffrage.
ECINet
The Election Commission's integrated digital platform, from which voter lists and election services are run in one place.
photo_note: Opposition leaders raise their hands in support of the motion at the symbolic parliament at 10 Rajaji Marg

h: 'No other way left': a parliament of 21 parties, and charges of sedition
dek: According to ThePrint, the symbolic parliament adopted a six-point motion demanding Gyanesh Kumar's immediate removal, and several speakers asked for him to be tried for sedition.
body: ThePrint's Isha Mishra writes that 21 parties of the Congress-led INDIA bloc gathered at Kharge's home and adopted a six-point motion to remove Gyanesh Kumar, in the first symbolic parliament of its kind. The report mentions no vote or count.

Rahul Gandhi said the opposition was left with no option but to take this step. He claimed that 13.3 crore names were deleted in the SIR, about 15 per cent of voters, while the margin in the 2024 election was only 3 per cent. He said 'vote chori' (vote theft) will not go unpunished.

The motion carries charges of changing Form 6, centralising the lists through ERONet and ECINet, and keeping two Commissioners out of decisions. According to the report, at least 14 objections had been recorded on this. It also includes charges of benefiting the Commissioner's family.

Among the speakers, Sagarika Ghose of the Trinamool said Bengal's 2026 election was 'stolen'. Arvind Sawant of Shiv Sena (Uddhav) raised the question of 40 lakh votes being cast between 4 and 5 pm in Maharashtra in 2024 and the CCTV footage not being made available. Yogendra Yadav, Abhay Kushwaha of the RJD and Sudama Prasad of the CPI(ML) accused the Commissioner of a conspiracy to break the country, and demanded his arrest and a sedition case. John Brittas, E.T. Mohammed Basheer and Nikhil Dey also spoke.
nazar: Twenty-one parties coming to one table is news in itself. But a word like sedition makes the allegation heavier, not the evidence. The opposition's strength lies in figures and documents, and sticking to them will serve it best.
sawal: If 15 per cent of names were deleted, who set the margin at 3 per cent?
ref: Form 6
The application form for getting a new name added to the electoral roll, which falls under the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960.
photo_note: Rahul Gandhi speaking at the symbolic parliament

h: Kharge's target at the mock parliament; in reply, the BJP recalled Nehru and Patel
dek: According to Patrika, Kharge said the opposition has no personal enmity with Gyanesh Kumar and that it is about the dignity of an institution, while the BJP hit back on Patel's birth anniversary.
body: According to Patrika, while moving the motion Kharge said the Election Commission is running on the direct instructions of the Prime Minister and the Home Minister, and that the Chief Election Commissioner is part of it. He also said the opposition has no personal enmity with Gyanesh Kumar and only wants to protect the dignity of the institution.

Kharge alleged that since 2014 the government has stayed in power through electoral bonds, the ED and CBI, defections and toppling governments, and is now doing 'vote chori'. He claimed there are hundreds of such examples, though according to the report he named none.

He questioned the 2023 law that sets the appointment and service conditions of the Chief Election Commissioner. This law was passed in December 2023, when 145 opposition MPs were suspended. He said this very law gives the Commissioner more protection than needed, and that this is why the notice from 193 MPs seven months ago was rejected without consideration.

On the BJP's behalf, spokesperson Sambit Patra held a press conference and hit back. On the birth anniversary of Sardar Patel, he argued that 'vote chori' had happened right after Independence, when Nehru was chosen over Patel, who had the Congress's support for the post of Prime Minister. There was no reaction from the Election Commission.
nazar: The BJP's reply was about history, not about the charges. The question of crores of deleted names is not answered by a party meeting in 1946. If the Commission stays silent and the ruling side keeps changing the subject, suspicion will only deepen.
sawal: What answer does the 1946 debate give on the question of deleted names?
ref: The 2023 Election Commissioner law
This law removed the Chief Justice from the panel that selects Commissioners, put a Union minister in his place, and gave Commissioners protection from lawsuits.

h: Names deleted by computer from Delhi, and now it is Ramlila Maidan's turn
dek: According to The India Daily, Kharge warned that anyone sitting in Delhi can remove names from the list by computer, and Rahul Gandhi called for a 'Chalo Delhi' march on 1 November.
body: According to this report, Meira Kumar said as chair that the voter is the pivot of an election, and that democracy is hurt if even one eligible citizen is stopped from voting. She said the bloc will meet next and plan to bring a motion in Parliament to remove the Commissioner, and that Kharge will take it forward.

Kharge said that today anyone sitting in Delhi can quietly remove names from the voter list by computer. He stressed protecting the voting rights of women, young people and weaker sections, and repeated the point about the rejected notice from 193 MPs and the law passed on the day 145 MPs were suspended.

The report says the event was to be held on Friday, but because of rain it was postponed to Saturday, by consensus, for the convenience of senior leaders. The whole event was called a symbolic impeachment.

Rahul Gandhi called for a 'Chalo Delhi' march on 1 November. The march was to begin at noon from Minto Road crossing and reach Ramlila Maidan via Connaught Place and Ajmeri Gate. Citing police sources, the report says no application had been received for the Connaught Place route, while permission for a rally at Ramlila Maidan had already been given.
nazar: The symbolic parliament was also preparation for the next day's march on the street. The real test now is how the police and administration behave on the rally route, and when the opposition brings the motion it has promised in Parliament.
sawal: How many voters' fate can one computer decide?
ref: Ramlila Maidan
A historic ground in Delhi that has hosted big public gatherings, from the 1975 rally against the Emergency to the Anna movement.

h: 'This is not a mock parliament, it is the people's impeachment'
dek: According to ETV Bharat's live blog, before the event Congress said it was not given permission, and Pawan Khera said civil society outside the bloc also wants to join.
body: ETV Bharat's live blog gives an account of the hours before the event. The programme was set for 3:30 pm at 10 Rajaji Marg. The planned format was that Meira Kumar would chair, Kharge would move the motion, one speaker from each party would speak, and Rahul Gandhi would give the closing speech, after which the motion would be considered 'passed'.

Congress said it was not given permission to hold the event, which is why it took place inside the party president's home. Rahul Gandhi alleged that Home Minister Amit Shah is trying to stop people from coming to Delhi.

Around noon, word came that the event had been rescheduled. Rahul Gandhi repeated his invitation to political parties, civil society, journalists and ordinary people to join the 1 November march to Ramlila Maidan. According to him, both the impeachment and the march are against the 'demolition of democracy' that he accuses Modi, Shah and Gyanesh Kumar of.

Congress MP Pawan Khera said it is wrong to call this a mock parliament, that it is the public impeachment of Gyanesh Kumar, and that besides the bloc, people from civil society also want to join it. The blog's last entry was made before the event began, so it has no account of the outcome.
nazar: The allegation of being denied permission gave even this symbolic event the shape of a protest. When there is no place for debate, people turn the courtyards of their homes into a parliament. That is not a good sign for any government.
sawal: When permission is denied, does a courtyard become a parliament?
ref: Pawan Khera
Head of the Congress media and publicity department, and one of the main faces who put the party's side.

h: Attacking Iran after the election: Trump's gamble will backfire
dek: Branko Marcetic argues that a fresh attack on Iran after the midterm election will neither make Iran bend nor make America safe, but may push the whole world into a big crisis.
body: Jacobin's Branko Marcetic writes that after the American midterm election on 3 November, the Trump administration is preparing to attack Iran again. Citing the Wall Street Journal, he says the plan is for a short but sharp war, striking infrastructure, missile stockpiles and nuclear sites. The final decision is pending, but Senator Chris Murphy has called it madness.

According to the writer, this attack will not achieve the aim of forcing Iran into an even weaker deal. After many Iranian officials were killed at the start of the war, hardliners opposed to talks have grown stronger there, and they have begun to see a nuclear weapon as a guarantee of defence. Bombs barely reach deeply buried sites. Meanwhile ordinary Iranians are bearing the burden of nearly 90 per cent inflation and at least 270 billion dollars of destroyed infrastructure.

Marcetic also considers Netanyahu's role important, as he keeps pushing for a new war. Israel's election gave no clear majority, and if no government is formed he stays on as caretaker. The writer hints that in such a case a war could prop up his coalition.

The danger is not limited to Iran. Iranian officials have said that if there is an attack, the Gulf's energy sites, ports, power grids and water treatment plants will be targets, which could trap the world in recession and a refugee crisis.

The writer's conclusion is simple: Trump should accept the same deal agreed early this year, and take the criticism. The White House says Iran is about to kneel, but according to the writer today's Iran is more dangerous, because it feels it has less left to lose.
nazar: According to Iran, four tankers have caught fire after hitting mines in Hormuz. Such reports show how fragile this pause is. India's rupee is already under pressure, and a new war means costlier oil, a weaker rupee, and unease among lakhs of families who work in the Gulf.
The most stinging point is that one country's election count is deciding when bombs fall on another. Those who speak of peace should openly question this timetable.
sawal: Will an election date decide whether Hormuz burns?
ref: Strait of Hormuz
The narrow sea route between Iran and Oman through which a large share of the world's oil trade passes. Any blockage here shakes oil prices.
Midterm election
Elections to the legislature held in the middle of a US president's term. They decide who controls the two houses of Congress.

h: Protection before a settlement: the call for a security force in Palestine
dek: Sameer Jaber says the survival of Palestinian society cannot wait for a political settlement, so an international protection force is needed now.
body: Palestinian activist and researcher Sameer Jaber argues that the world's diplomacy has so far been stuck on a political solution, while the real and urgent question is how Palestinians can stay alive on their land. In his view, since October 2023 the pace of occupation and settlement has been so fast that the basic supports of living, namely homes, healthcare, education, jobs and security, are being broken one by one.

He builds the picture with figures. More than 74,000 people have been killed in Gaza, about 81 per cent of buildings are destroyed and 19 lakh people are homeless, living in tents. Only 19 of 36 hospitals are somehow functioning, and according to UNICEF 98 per cent of schools are broken or damaged. Unemployment in Gaza is above 90 per cent.

The West Bank is no different. Citing Al-Haq, the writer says that between 2023 and 2025, 46 communities were uprooted, the camps of Jenin, Nur Shams and Tulkarm were badly broken, and around 5,000 people were displaced in Hebron. There are demolition or stop-work orders on 84 schools, farmers have not been able to harvest for three years, and unemployment has doubled to 29.5 per cent.

That is why Jaber demands an international protection force. He sees its legal basis in the International Court of Justice's advisory opinions, which called the occupation illegal and placed on Israel the responsibility to let aid reach Gaza. A US veto in the Security Council is almost certain, so he suggests the General Assembly's 1950 'Uniting for Peace' route, which South Africa, the Arab League and the countries of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation can initiate.

The writer is clear that this force should not be like Hebron's old international team that only kept recording excesses. Its job should be to protect people, to be a wall between the settlements and the settlers, and to stop attacks.
nazar: The weight of Jaber's argument is that he sets aside the long debate about peace talks and puts the question of saving lives first. For the children of a school with a bulldozer standing at its gate, a map of some future border is meaningless.

Since independence, India has made a place among the largest troop contributors to UN peacekeeping missions. This legacy of the Global South creates hope that it will not stay silent on such an initiative.
sawal: Whom could observers who only watched in Hebron protect?
ref: Uniting for Peace
A 1950 resolution of the UN General Assembly. When the Security Council is stalled by a veto, the Assembly can recommend collective action.
International team in Hebron (TIPH)
International observers stationed in Hebron from 1994 to 2019. They had only the authority to watch and report.

h: Injustice makes the body sick, not just society
dek: Rafia Zakaria says that in an unequal society the burden of daily vigilance and injustice falls directly on health, and that the cure is collective, not personal.
body: Lawyer and human rights activist Rafia Zakaria begins with the everyday life of a chaotic metropolis like Karachi. Until he reaches the office, a person is on alert every moment, battling traffic, reckless drivers, filth and dangers. The rich have the shield of drivers, air conditioners, generators and private healthcare, but according to the writer this shield lets them do only one thing: treat the injustice around them as something distant, and see their comfort as their right and others' suffering as fate.

She draws on 'Weathering', a book by the American researcher Arline Geronimus, which argues that the stress of dealing with injustice every day wears down both body and mind. The weakest pay the highest price, but in an unequal society nobody is spared.

The writer pays special attention to women. In a patriarchal system a woman is always on the defensive. If the in-laws' demands are not met, marriage becomes dangerous, infertility becomes an excuse for divorce or a second wife, and children increase her dependence further. She cites a 2021 study according to which 37 per cent of pregnant women in Pakistan were depressed before childbirth and 30 per cent after, and she links this to domestic violence and strained relationships. Men are not untouched by it either.

Constant stress disturbs hormones, raises blood pressure and creates inflammation in the body, which raises the risk of chronic illness and early death. That is why the writer says that what really decides health is not personal habits or money but how a society treats justice and the dignity of life. The treatment of the poor, treating women as property, abuse of children, and fates decided by caste and wealth are all symptoms of this same disease.
Her biggest worry is that people have accepted injustice as unchangeable. Exercise, dieting or quitting cigarettes is not the cure for it; the cure lies in collective action.
nazar: This applies just as much to India's cities and towns. The fear of dowry, domestic violence and caste humiliation are not only social questions but public health questions, and they cannot be seen apart from the hospital budget.
Zakaria's point also holds up a mirror to the 'wellness' industry that offers private shopping as the cure for every sorrow. The fight for justice is really the fight for health.
sawal: Whose blood pressure records the fear of a Karachi road?
ref: Weathering
The theory and book of American public health researcher Arline Geronimus. According to it, the constant stress of discrimination and poverty ages the body early and makes it ill.

h: A lock on investing abroad to save the rupee?
dek: Shoaib Daniyal argues that the news of a curb on money sent abroad shows both the economy's weakness and that the BJP treats the middle class as its sure vote.
body: In Scroll's newsletter 'The India Fix', Shoaib Daniyal begins with a Zee Business report. According to the report, the Reserve Bank is considering changes to the Liberalised Remittance Scheme: RBI permission would be needed to send money to buy property abroad, and a limit of 50 lakh rupees would be placed on other remittances. According to the writer, this would directly mean ordinary Indians cannot put money into foreign shares, which reminds him of the licence-permit raj.

The report rests on an unnamed source, so the writer treats it not as a decision but as a balloon, floated to see how much people erupt. The background is serious. The rupee is near a record low against the dollar and repeatedly about to touch 100. Since June the Reserve Bank has been selling dollars to stem the fall, and according to one report reserves have dropped by about 65 billion dollars in six weeks.

The writer reminds us that before 2014 Modi launched sharp attacks on the Manmohan Singh government over the falling rupee, and the irony is that under his rule the rupee has often been among Asia's weakest currencies. Meanwhile the country's stock market is stagnant, foreign investors are pulling money out, and that is why the middle class had increased its investment abroad. The proposed curb will shut this route too.

The most interesting part is political. Citing Saurabh Mukherjea's book, the writer says that amid falling jobs, stagnant salaries and rising debt, the Indian middle class is becoming poorer for the first time since 1991. Yet it has no political power, because a large part of it is upper-caste Hindu, which is the BJP's surest vote bank. This loyalty rests not on economics but on identity and ideology, so according to the writer the BJP feels no need to fear policies that hit its pocket.
nazar: Daniyal's analysis breaks the illusion that loyalty in voting automatically protects one's interests. A section taken for granted has the cheapest grievances for those in power.
But the real blow will fall on those who never had the option of investing abroad: the price of costly oil and a weak rupee is paid first by the kitchens of workers and farmers.
sawal: Who will worry about the pocket of the sure-vote middle class?
ref: Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS)
The Reserve Bank's scheme running since 2004, under which Indian residents can send money abroad each year up to a set limit. Through it people pay for study, travel and investment in foreign shares.

h: Metros and highways are being built, but who will connect the relationships?
dek: Viren Brahmbhatt says India is building pieces of infrastructure fast, but nobody has a map of how these pieces relate to each other.
body: Viren Brahmbhatt, an architect and urban designer working in New York, argues that India is building parts like metros, highways and riverfronts far faster than it is worrying about how they will connect with each other. A city succeeds not through good infrastructure but when infrastructure, land, housing, jobs, public spaces and institutions work together. According to World Bank estimates, India's urban population could grow from about 48 crore in 2020 to 95 crore by 2050.

Governments like projects that are visible, countable, and have a budget and a deadline. The trouble is that each project is examined separately, while roads, housing and jobs together change land prices and the whole pattern of commuting. Municipal boundaries no longer match the areas where people live and work, and transport, land and water are split among different departments. The 74th Constitutional Amendment also lies unfinished.

The writer gives two examples. In Bengaluru, jobs have clustered in a few areas, but housing, transport and environmental protection have been left behind. In Mumbai land is scarce and housing costly, so the formal economy rests on workers who cannot pay rent for formal housing. Pushing domestic workers, delivery workers and street vendors aside in the name of 'formalisation' raises both their travel and their costs. According to the writer, informality is the answer to the failure of the formal system.

Dense settlement is not a solution by itself either: without transport it becomes jams, and without cheap housing it becomes exclusion. The writer suggests that the question should change from 'which project to build' to 'which relationship to build'. Neither the old rigid master plans, nor growth left only to the market, but a framework that decides where development should happen and which settlements must be protected from being uprooted.
nazar: This piece reminds us that the politics of cutting ribbons on shining metros and expressways often leaves out of the count the people without whom no metropolis runs for a day. Domestic workers and street vendors are not counted as stakeholders in any project report.
The 74th Amendment promised real power to local bodies. Without fulfilling it, every talk of a 'smart' city is incomplete.
sawal: How many hours a day does a Mumbai domestic worker lose commuting?
ref: 74th Constitutional Amendment
The 1992 amendment that gave municipalities constitutional status and spoke of handing functions like urban planning to local bodies. In many states its implementation is still incomplete.

h: WHO should declare the climate crisis a health emergency
dek: Four public health researchers argue that the climate crisis is killing people today, and that the World Health Organization should declare it a public health emergency of international concern.
by: Nicholas Brink, Fortunate Machingura, Matthew Chersich and Rob Butler
body: Four researchers linked to South Africa's University of the Witwatersrand, the University of Manchester and the London School of Economics write that the climate crisis is not a fear of the future but today's reality. The northern hemisphere endured yet another record summer of heat and extreme weather, while the south has heatwaves, floods, fires and drought, and El Nino has fuelled it further. In Nepal floods uprooted entire communities, in Spain a forest fire took everything from more than two and a half lakh people, and in European cities more than 50,000 deaths last summer were reported as heat-related.

The authors' own research on heat in Africa showed a deep effect on the health of pregnant women and unborn children. Communities in South Africa understand their danger, but they have no means of protection.

The authors' complaint is with institutions. The World Health Organization has for decades called climate change the biggest health threat of this century, yet the global health system is not ready, and the responsibility has been left to slow, consensus-driven climate negotiations. The 1.5 degree target has slipped out of reach.

That is why they demand that the WHO declare it a public health emergency of international concern. In their view the climate crisis meets most of its conditions, and this would mobilise political will, money and a shared strategy. A recent report estimates 4,51,000 additional deaths from heat between June 2026 and February 2027, equal to the deaths in the first six months of Covid.

The elderly, pregnant women, children and the chronically ill are at greatest risk, and so are those in the Global South who have the smallest share in pollution. The health ministries of Senegal, Namibia and Zimbabwe have already backed this demand. The article first appeared in The Conversation and Down To Earth republished it.
nazar: In India, heat now kills farm workers, construction workers and street vendors every year, but the framework to record it as a disaster and pay compensation is still weak. If the WHO makes such a declaration, pressure on governments will grow to treat heat as a health crisis and arrange working hours, water and shade.
The demand matters also because it looks at climate not only in terms of carbon but in terms of people's bodies and lives.
sawal: Are four and a half lakh estimated deaths not enough to call it an emergency?
ref: Public Health Emergency of International Concern (PHEIC)
The World Health Organization's highest alert, issued under the International Health Regulations. It has been declared for Covid-19 and mpox.

h: New board for gig workers, seats filled by Sangh-linked bodies
dek: Most recognised unions were left out of the National Social Security Board formed for gig and platform workers.
body: On Friday the Union Ministry of Labour and Employment notified the formation of the National Social Security Board for gig and platform workers. Formed under the Code on Social Security, the board's job is to make welfare schemes for these workers, monitor them and give recommendations to the government.

The board has 40 members, nominated by the government for three years. Seven seats are for labour unions and seven for employers' representatives. The remaining members are drawn from various government departments and Parliament.

Citing the Indian Express, Maktoob reports that of these fourteen, six seats went to two organisations linked to the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh. Of the unions' seven, three are with the Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh, and of the employers' seven, three are with Laghu Udyog Bharati, which works for small and medium industries. Most of the twelve central unions recognised by the government got no place. Neither CITU nor AITUC has a representative on the board.

According to the report, the representation of states is one-sided too. Only Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh, Gujarat and West Bengal got places, which the report describes as BJP-ruled states, while states with opposition governments are left out. The report carries no response from the government or these organisations.
nazar: Lakhs of people who deliver and drive cabs have been demanding social security for years. If the board meant to carry their voice is filled with organisations of a single ideology, schemes will be made less for workers' needs and more for the government's convenience. Keeping away from the table the unions that fought for these workers on the street creates suspicion, not trust.
sawal: Whom will a board without CITU and AITUC listen to?
ref: Code on Social Security, 2020
One of the four labour codes. For the first time it gave legal recognition to gig and platform workers and provided for a welfare board for them.
Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh
A trade union founded in 1955 by Dattopant Thengadi, considered part of the Sangh Parivar.

h: Notice over one article, and twelve years of archive vanish
dek: A hosting company shut down journalist Paranjoy Guha Thakurta's website without notice, and at the root are legal notices from the founder of Indiabulls.
body: Senior journalist Paranjoy Guha Thakurta's website paranjoy.in, which held twelve years of his reporting and writing, was taken off the internet on 28 October. In his statement of 31 October, Thakurta said the hosting company Hostinger suspended his entire account without telling him beforehand and without hearing him.

The matter began in August, when lawyers for Indiabulls founder Sameer Gehlaut sent a notice demanding that one article be removed within 24 to 48 hours. Thakurta was later made a defendant in a lawsuit, and on 24 October the court issued an injunction. According to Thakurta, he was preparing to challenge that order in a higher court when the whole site went down. His lawyers are now looking for a way to fight both the injunction and the suspension.

The report recalls that Thakurta has long clashed with big corporate houses. In 2017, after an article on the Adani group was taken down, he resigned as editor of Economic and Political Weekly. In 2021, a court in Kutch issued an arrest warrant against him over an article from that same period. Reliance has also sent him notices.

People who work on press freedom have criticised the move. Their question is how an order about one article can be used as an excuse to wipe out an entire archive. Hostinger has so far given no public explanation for its decision.
nazar: This is a new and cheap way of censorship: the government need not issue any order, and one notice and a private company's fear are enough. If businessmen with big lawyers can make years of a journalist's work vanish overnight whenever they like, investigative journalism becomes riskier still. Courts should see that a bar on one article does not become a bar on an entire voice.
sawal: The dispute was over one article, so what was the fault of the thousands of other pages?
ref: Injunction
An interim court order that stops some action until the case is decided, such as publishing an article.
Paranjoy Guha Thakurta
An investigative journalist on economic and corporate matters, author of books such as 'Gas Wars' and former editor of EPW.

h: October cleanup on Instagram: videos removed, reach cut
dek: According to SFLC data, 174 posts and 59 accounts were blocked in India on Instagram alone this month, and the reason was often not even given.
body: According to this Newslaundry investigation, restrictions on social media in India rose sharply in October. The Software Freedom Law Centre (SFLC) recorded blocks on 268 posts and 83 accounts this month across Meta, X, Reddit and YouTube. Instagram was at the top, where 174 posts and 59 accounts were blocked. In July, only 51 posts were removed across the three platforms combined.

Those affected include journalist and teacher Raghav Trivedi, whose eight videos were removed within 48 hours and whose new videos are blocked in India within half an hour. By his account, his reach fell from ten crore to three crore in a month. Maolitics' page was blocked in India on 10 October and returned a few days later, while its reporter Geetanjali Dubey is getting by on a small backup account after her personal account was shut.

SFLC lawyer Angela Thomas alleges that Meta is removing posts by machine, and that content with words like 'ECI', 'protest' and 'SIR' is being targeted. Two LiveLaw videos were also blocked citing a 'legal request'. Delhi Police DCP Gaurav Tyagi admitted that the police sent Meta several requests last month.

The complaint route goes first to Meta's officers and then to the government's appellate committee, whose independence lawyer Krishnesh Bapat questions. On 29 October the Delhi High Court said that the suspension of an Instagram account cannot be challenged through a writ petition. Meta did not respond to the report.
nazar: When neither the reason for a ban is given nor the order shown, challenging it becomes almost impossible. After newspapers and TV, this platform is now the support of small independent journalists, and quietly cutting their reach is no less dangerous than direct censorship. Making public every request sent under the IT rules would be the minimum accountability.
sawal: From ten crore to three crore: who cut the reach, and on whose order?
ref: Grievance Appellate Committee
A government-formed committee under the IT Rules 2021 where a user unhappy with a social media company's decision can appeal.
sflc.in
A Delhi organisation that provides data and legal help on digital rights, internet shutdowns and online censorship.

h: Police enter newsroom in Nepal, journalists detained
dek: The day after a report on an alleged meeting between a judge and a power broker, several journalists were picked up in Kathmandu, and no one was told why.
body: Nepal Police detained at least three journalists on Friday, 30 October, and tried to detain a few more. They were released a few hours later, but the police gave no reason. Police stayed about two hours at the office of the Nepali daily Naya Patrika to catch editor Khagendra Pant and senior reporter Nabaraj Mainali. In the end they left after asking them to appear at the Cyber Bureau.

Bishomani Subedi, a reporter of the online portal Nepal Press, was picked up, and its editor-in-chief Matrika Poudel and chairman Bindu Raj Lamsal were called in by the Cyber Bureau and taken into custody. An attempt was also made to detain journalists of another portal, Deopost.

A day earlier, Naya Patrika had reported that Inam Sapkota, regarded as a broker in the corridors of power, had asked Supreme Court judge Hari Prasad Phuyal to dismiss a case involving the interests of Prime Minister Balendra Shah. Some newspapers had also printed speculation that the police chief would be removed, which police headquarters called baseless.

The Prime Minister's Office distanced itself from the arrests and directed the police to release the journalists and not to enter newsrooms. The ruling Rastriya Swatantra Party also called it an attack on press freedom. Just before the holiday, the Press Council Nepal expressed concern over arrests without a warrant and demanded that the legal basis be made public.
nazar: Nepal's new government emerged from a youth movement, one of whose big demands was accountability. In that very period, a police raid on journalists who exposed a meeting between a judge and a broker points in the opposite direction. The Prime Minister's Office says it had no knowledge, which raises a bigger question: on whose say is the police acting?
sawal: The story went to a judge's door, so why did the police go to the newsroom?
ref: Press Council Nepal
A statutory body in Nepal that looks into journalism's code of conduct and complaints about news reports.
Cyber Bureau
The cybercrime unit of Nepal Police, which is accused of recently bypassing the Press Council and handling media cases itself.

h: Suspected for 22 years, Kasem Ali declared Indian by tribunal
dek: A Foreigners Tribunal declared Kasem Ali, who pulls a handcart in Assam's Bongaigaon, a citizen, but his wife is still a D-voter.
body: Foreigners Tribunal No. 1 has declared Kasem Ali, who supports his family by pulling a handcart in Assam's Bongaigaon, an Indian citizen. With this judgment of 25 October 2026, a case ended that was registered in 2004 on the orders of the Superintendent of Border Police. The surprising part is that Kasem received the notice eighteen years later, in March 2022.

Kasem was born in 1968 in Dhupuri village under Manikpur police station. In his written statement he said he was born in Assam itself and never came from East Pakistan or Bangladesh. As proof he submitted 18 documents: the 1966 and 1971 voter lists carrying his parents' names, a land lease in his father's name, a 1975 school certificate, and voter lists from 1997 to now. A revenue department employee testified and confirmed the lease.

The defence said that the investigating officer neither visited the house, nor took a statement, nor questioned witnesses. Differences in the spelling of names, such as Kasem and Kasam, were called clerical errors. The tribunal held that Kasem had discharged the burden of proving his citizenship under Section 9 of the Foreigners Act. With the help of Citizens for Justice and Peace, lawyer Dewan Abdur Rahim fought the case.
But the family's trouble is not over. Kasem's wife Suratan Khatun was declared a D-voter in 2019 and cannot vote until 2029. Her husband's judgment does not resolve her separate case.
nazar: A man held papers going back to 1966, yet he had to live for twenty-two years like a stranger on his own land, and the notice reached him only after eighteen years. In Assam the burden of citizenship is placed on the one who can least afford a lawyer. When will the investigating officer who writes a report without visiting the house be held accountable?
sawal: Parents in the 1966 voter list, and still twenty-two years of suspicion?
ref: Foreigners Tribunal
Quasi-judicial bodies in Assam that decide whether a person is to be treated as a foreigner. Under Section 9 of the Foreigners Act, the burden of proving citizenship lies on the accused.
D-voter
A 'doubtful voter', someone whose citizenship is questioned. Such a person's right to vote is held back until the tribunal's decision comes.

h: Newborn breaths go out again in Attappadi: twelve deaths, old questions
dek: Twelve newborn deaths in recent months in Attappadi, a tribal area of Kerala, have reopened the old crisis of malnutrition, land and maternal health.
body: In the past few months, twelve newborn babies have died in the Attappadi area of Kerala's Palakkad district, ten of them from tribal families. The state government has formed expert teams to investigate. Health Minister K. Muraleedharan says the deaths were caused not by negligence in treatment but by serious illnesses present from birth. A seven-member team from medical colleges will examine pregnant women and children under five, and will go to the settlements.

Figures from tribal activists tell a long story: 124 newborn deaths since 2011, about 300 miscarriages and 90 stillbirths since 2012. In 2013, the deaths of 47 children here drew the nation's attention. According to Rajendra Prasad, president of the tribal organisation Thampu, eight of the last ten deaths were linked to serious heart disease, and despite about 490 crore rupees spent on malnutrition, no solid scientific study has been done.

The report lists deeper causes: anaemia among pregnant women, newborns weighing under two kilos, late registration of pregnancy and sickle cell anaemia. In the 1940s, tribal people were about 95 percent of the area's population, and today they are 44 percent. Loss of land, poverty and cheap liquor are making things worse.

Politics has also heated up. The opposition LDF observed a black day in Attappadi on 31 October, while Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes Welfare Minister K.A. Thulasi said that the coordination committee set up by the previous government never met after 2023, and that community kitchens fell from 174 to 28.
nazar: Attappadi makes headlines every few years and is then forgotten. Governments change, allegations change, but the question of the tribal mother's plate and her land stays where it was. Until the inquiry goes beyond the hospital to the settlement, the kitchen and the land papers, these deaths will remain just a statistic.
sawal: 490 crore was spent, so why did community kitchens fall to 28?
ref: Attappadi
A hilly tribal area of Palakkad district where the Irula, Muduga and Kurumba communities live. Infant deaths here have repeatedly been in the news since 2013.
Sickle cell anaemia
An inherited blood disease in which red cells become sickle shaped. It is found more often in many tribal communities.

h: Dewas's ponds: water has returned, but not to every farm
dek: This Down To Earth report says the farm ponds begun two decades ago in Malwa's Dewas raised incomes, but the accounting for small farmers and for groundwater is still incomplete.
body: Until about twenty years ago, Dewas district in Madhya Pradesh's Malwa region faced a severe water shortage. Citing an IWMI study, the report says tubewells in the district rose from 3,887 in 1990 to 23,119 by 2009-10, and about 82 percent of irrigation depended on groundwater.

In 2006, on the initiative of the then collector Umakant Umrao, the administration asked farmers to set aside a part of their land for a pond, gave technical advice and got them bank loans. It began with 40 big farmers, and about two thousand ponds were built in fourteen months. Today the estimate is 30 to 35 thousand ponds, though there is no official count.

The benefit is visible. Rainwater was held back, water returned to wells and many farmers began taking a second crop. Along with wheat, oilseeds and chia, fish farming and dairy also raised earnings. According to a farmer in Tonk Kalan, people bought vehicles, cattle and brick houses with the earnings from the ponds.

But the report also shows the limits of this success. The model favours farmers who have land and access to credit and who can give up ten to twenty percent of their field. A farmer in Tonk Kalan says that for a family with two acres, a pond means losing a third of its food security.

Groundwater has not improved much either. In the Central Ground Water Board's 2023 assessment, the district's extraction was 79.99 percent and Dewas was counted in the 'over-exploited' category, and in Dewas block, withdrawal was higher than the annual recharge, at 110.88 percent. The writer argues that counting ponds shows the scale of conservation, but not whether the water under the ground is returning. For that, solid data on well levels and pumping depth is needed.
nazar: Dewas shows that when farmers treat water as their own responsibility and the administration backs them, farming can recover even in a dry area. But a scheme whose condition is giving up a piece of land reaches first those who have land to give up.

The real lesson for states struggling with this year's El Nino drought is that routes such as shared ponds, panchayat land and collective water management should be built for small and marginal farmers, and that an honest account of groundwater should be kept.
sawal: Where will a farmer with two acres find land for a pond?
ref: Malwa
The western plateau region of Madhya Pradesh, covering districts such as Indore, Ujjain and Dewas. Once considered rich in water, it fell into a groundwater crisis in the tubewell era.
Over-exploited block
A Central Ground Water Board category in which the groundwater drawn from an area each year is more than its recharge. In such areas the water level keeps falling.

h: The Palestine team that had not a single Palestinian
dek: This Al Jazeera World film opens up the story of the team that took the field under the name 'Palestine' in the 1934 World Cup qualifiers, a team with no place for Arab Palestinian players.
body: In the qualifying matches for the 1934 football World Cup, to be held in fascist Italy, a team took the field under the name 'Palestine'. Al Jazeera World's film of about 47 minutes, 'Palestine: The Lost Team', released on 7 October 2026, is about this forgotten team. The film's central fact is startling: this team did not have a single Arab Palestinian player.

According to the film, the team, formed during the British Mandate, was chosen mainly from the Jewish sports movement. That is, the majority Arab population of the land in whose name the team played was kept off its field. The film sees this not just as a sporting tale but as the beginning of a long fight over identity and recognition.

Through old records, conversations with historians and the qualifier matches played against Egypt in 1934, the film examines how British rule, the Zionist organisation and the policy of keeping Palestinians out together shaped this team. These matches played on the field become a mirror of the politics of that era.

The film argues that the football association formed in that period went on to become Israel's football association. On the other side, Palestinian football was first scattered by revolt and war, and then by the Nakba of 1948, when lakhs of Palestinians were driven from their homes.
The story after that is one of insistence on return. The film shows that Palestinians struggled for decades to regain their place in world football, and finally won FIFA recognition in 1998.

Through sport, the film raises a question that is even sharper today amid the devastation of Gaza: who decides the name of a people, and who has the right to represent them? Beginning with an old football match, the story reaches colonialism, dispossession and the politics of identity.
nazar: The deepest wound of colonialism is in taking away name and representation even before taking away land. This 1934 team shows that the very people in whose name decisions are made can be kept out of the table and the field.

Readers in South Asia will recognise this story: even in the colonial period, institutions and 'representatives' here were often shaped by the wishes of the rulers. The return of Palestinian football is a reminder that the fight for identity is long, but does not end.
sawal: Whom did a team without Palestinians represent?
ref: British Mandate Palestine
British rule over Palestine from 1920 to 1948 after the First World War, under a League of Nations mandate. In this period the conflict between Jewish settlements and the Arab population deepened.
Nakba
Arabic for 'catastrophe'. Palestinians remember by this name the expulsion of about seven lakh Palestinians and the emptying of hundreds of their villages with the creation of Israel in 1948.

h: 'Alochana' poetry issue: sixty poets, divided opinion
dek: Reading the three-volume poetry special issue of the magazine 'Alochana' on Sammukh, senior poet Satyapal Sehgal counts the restlessness and strengths of new Hindi poetry.
body: The magazine 'Alochana' (Criticism) has brought out a special issue in three volumes on twenty-first century Hindi poetry, with poems by sixty contemporary poets and their answers to the editors' questions. Poet Satyapal Sehgal reads this issue on Sammukh. He says that many of the poets are very young, some still students, and that this generation seems to avoid copying ready-made opinions.

A large part of the article surveys the views of the young poets. Saumya Malviya regrets the decline of self-criticism, and Sapna Bhatt doubts that poetry alone, without some big social movement, can deal with today's crises. For Parvati Tirki, writing about love for the forest is itself a political act, and Mohan Mukt says the poetry of resistance needs a new, precise language because old symbols go stiff.

Has Hindi poetry moved ahead in the new century? According to Sehgal, such a varied anthology has come for the first time since the Nayi Kavita (New Poetry) movement. Bodhisattva, Hare Prakash Upadhyay and Vishnu Nagar are doubtful about the newest writing, while Vinod Kumar Shukla and Shubha see real progress in it.

The writer singles out some poets: Mohan Mukt's poem on a Dalit drummer from Uttarakhand, and Anamika Anu's poem that questions the women's sorrow hidden in the miniature painting tradition. He notes that the issue has five poets of Muslim background, whose poems speak of hardship, fear and humiliation, and he takes this as a sign of a larger social change.

Last comes the debate on social media: do reels and poster poems bring new readers or flatten poetry? Sehgal makes the interesting remark that these poets are critics of technology but have themselves been shaped by it. He praises the labour of editor Ashutosh Kumar and hopes for a fourth volume.
nazar: A debate over this issue's selection is already under way in Hindi, and Sehgal's reading is the other side of it. Its merit is that it treats the identity of poets not as something to count but as a mirror of a changing society. The appearance of Adivasi, Dalit and Muslim poets together is news of the widening of Hindi poetry's democracy, and in today's climate that is the most necessary thing.
sawal: Is a poem read on a reel smaller than a poem in a book?
ref: Alochana
An old Hindi critical magazine published by Rajkamal Prakashan, begun in 1951. Namvar Singh was also among its editors.
Nayi Kavita
The Hindi poetry movement of the 1950s and 60s, with which poets such as Agyeya, Muktibodh and Raghuveer Sahay were associated.

h: When will the wind change? The unfinished journey of equality in marriage
dek: The fourth instalment of Pallavi Vinod's 'Dampatya' series on Sammukh answers those who say marriage is no longer a burden for women.
body: Pallavi Vinod is writing on Sammukh about marriage and the relationship between women and men under the title 'Dampatya' (Married Life). After the third instalment, some people said that things have changed, that girls today are so outspoken that in-laws are afraid of them. The writer's reply is that such remarks often come from homes with sons, while homes with daughters are still only praying.

She does not deny change. A generation ago, women stayed veiled before their husbands; today they give opinions on the family and understand investments. But according to the writer, this is a change of understanding and ability, not of power. A capable woman's confidence stings many men, and they either shut their eyes or close the very window through which the light comes.

She tells two stories. A friend's husband rejected every suggestion saying he was the master of the house, and the friend chose to separate. A new daughter-in-law was praised for fifteen days, and then came taunts about her looks, a scolding for wanting to drive a car, and reminders that her family had asked for the match. Following the advice to keep quiet, she slid into depression.

Then she turns to the film 'Thappad'. The writer asks why a man who raises his hand to his wife does not raise it to his father, boss or mother. Excusing anger as stress is putting a seal on the thinking of ownership. Women who go to offices bear stress too.

The last part is about her grandmother's house, where the grandfather's feet were washed when he came home from the office. From the sons, this expectation passed on to the daughters-in-law. The daughters-in-law protested every time, and the result is that their sons did not pick up those habits. The writer concludes that every system begins and ends only with resistance.
nazar: The talk of domestic violence and unpaid household work often shrinks into figures; this article brings it into the kitchen and the sitting room. The most useful point is the last one: patriarchy does not reach the next generation by itself, it can be stopped. But the burden of keeping quiet is still put on the daughter-in-law, and as long as her parents' family also keeps saying 'adjust', the wind will change only slowly.
sawal: The daughters-in-law stopped the custom of washing feet, so why not the sons?
ref: Thappad (2020)
Anubhav Sinha's film in which Taapsee Pannu's character Amrita questions her whole marriage after her husband slaps her once.
Dampatya
Pallavi Vinod's series on Sammukh, being written on equality, companionship and conflict within marriage.

h: From library to lockup: a sardonic tale of a first protest
dek: On Hindwi Bela, Manish Tripathi tells with satire his experience of joining a Delhi protest on 11 October, being detained and jumping out of a police van.
body: On Sunday, 11 October, Manish Tripathi was sitting in the library of Delhi University's South Campus. According to the writer, a protest by Citizens for Justice and Peace (CJP) and several youth organisations was going on that day, and the news came that a girl who had joined the march had been detained. Leaving his books, he set out for the road. It was his first protest.

At Connaught Place there were about two hundred young people, and waiting for them were fifty or sixty journalists and YouTubers. Then a funny muddle appears: the group the writer took for Gen-Z protesters turned out to be the ruling party's youth wing, and the Congress Sewa Dal people also went and handed out water to the same crowd. The writer's jibe is that big channels broadcast live from such a distance that democracy comes into the frame, but not the lathi.

After walking around for an hour and a half and taking a few photographs, the writer too was caught. He describes the detention in three stages, from a pat to a slap and then to a boot, and he connects the bottle of water given afterwards with the idiom of 'killing with love'.

In the lockup cell, young men were stuffed in and it was hard to breathe. A Muslim woman from Sadar Bazaar was also there, who had come to see the leaders and was pleading for the release of her small children. When she spoke of the justice of the One above, a constable scolded her into silence. Then phones came out and a 'revolution' reel began to be made.

According to the writer, when the van slowed at a turn, several detainees opened the door and jumped out, the writer too. His conclusion carries both sarcasm and hope: in this era dissent is treated as a crime and a question as impertinence, and in such times the protest has become a ritual that keeps the memory of democracy alive, and hope is itself a resistance.
nazar: Behind the satire this is also testimony: beating in the van, young men stuffed into the lockup, and a scolding for a mother pleading for her children. These are the writer's own experiences and they should be investigated, but they show the pattern that many Delhi protesters have long complained of. Laughter here is a way of dealing with fear, and it should not be read lightly.
sawal: Why was she scolded for pleading to go back to her children?
ref: Gen-Z
The generation born roughly between 1997 and 2012, which grew up with social media. This year it is these young people who have been seen at the front of many Delhi protests.
Bela
Hindwi's prose section, where essays, letters, memoirs, reports and comments are published.

h: Veeraniyat-8: an evening of poetry in a city of fear
dek: On Hindwi Bela, Rajneesh Verma writes about the eighth edition of Jan Sanskriti Manch's annual poetry event 'Veeraniyat', with both praise and complaint.
body: In memory of the poet Viren Dangwal, Jan Sanskriti Manch holds a poetry reading in Delhi every year under the name 'Veeraniyat'. The eighth event was held on 9 October at Jawahar Bhawan. Rajneesh Verma's report places it in a time when, according to the writer, there were repeated arrests of protesters in the city and a fear like an undeclared Emergency. The Gen-Z movement was a big theme this time.

Ashutosh Kumar conducted the event, and it began with Ibbar Rabbi's poem about Delhi's crowded buses. Eight poets had been invited: Ibbar Rabbi, Anamika, Savita Singh, R. Chetankranti, Saumya Malviya, Parvati Tirki, Usama and Arbaaz Khan, but Rabbi could not come. A chorus sang Viren Dangwal's poem 'Hamara Samaj' (Our Society), to which the writer wished more time had been given.

Of Arbaaz Khan's two long poems, one was on children chirping in a mosque, a vision of the new generation against religious bigotry, and the other on the memory of a mason, in which the writer is reminded of Dhoomil's 'Mochiram'. Saumya Malviya's poems grapple with caste, the longing for freedom and the dictatorial tendency of power.

The report is not soft. The writer found Chetankranti's reading dull, the voice too low. The Adivasi words in Parvati Tirki's poems were sometimes beyond understanding, which the writer takes as the audience's own linguistic limit; forest, river and land come to her as companions. Usama's nazm had depth but less tightness, and Savita Singh's reading felt hurried, though the pain of a country turning into a market is clear in her poetry.

In the writer's view, the most effective reading of the evening was Anamika's, especially her poem on women who want to remain unmarried. The news that the metro was closing filled the audience with restlessness. The conclusion is that the event was a success, but weaker than last time, and the organisers should learn from it.
nazar: When speaking on the street is difficult, even poetry halls become places of public debate. From the children of the mosque to the Adivasi forest, the voices on the stage belong to the very India that today's politics pushes to the margins. The report's frank criticism is also good: even the poetry of resistance has to be good poetry.
sawal: If the metro closes, who comes to hear poetry?
ref: Viren Dangwal (1947-2015)
A Hindi poet who won the Sahitya Akademi Award for 'Dushchakra mein Srashta'. He taught in Bareilly all his life.
Jan Sanskriti Manch
A left-leaning organisation of writers and artists, formed in 1985, which holds cultural events across the country.

h: Religion in an age of reason: not rejection, a case for reform
dek: Vishal Kumar's essay on Hindwi Bela says it is wrong to treat religion as the enemy of reason and that today's religious frenzy is its corrupted form, for which the cure is reform.
body: Vishal Kumar's essay begins with a picture from farming: land left fallow for long gets taken over by encroachers and the soil loses its strength. The writer applies the same to India's religious and cultural tradition, whose identity, he says, powerful groups today want to fix by force.

He lists two pressures. One is external, the colonial gaze, which in different forms kept cutting Indians off from their culture. The other is internal, which sows thorny acacia in the empty land in the name of religion and culture. At the same time he is also angry with those critics who borrow foreign frameworks to attack their own tradition.

The writer distinguishes between dharma and 'religion'. Religion revolves around God, institutions and ritual, while dharma is about upholding, that is, a moral responsibility. According to the writer, the big names of the freedom struggle, Gandhi, Vivekananda, Tagore, Tilak and Nehru, did not reject dharma, and even the rationalist Ambedkar placed the dharma of principles above the dharma of rules.

The writer calls today's religious surge a corrupted form, whose marks are corridors, trusts, parties and 'dharma-raksha' squads.
